newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexico pays back U.S., sheds crisis stigma.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexico pays back U.S., sheds crisis stigma.

text.p: Mexico took a big step on Wednesday to shed the stigma of crisis by announcing it would pay off three years ahead of schedule the remainder of a $12.5 billion emergency bailout from the U.S. Treasury.

In a move trumpeted heartily by both the Clinton administration and Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, the Mexican government said it had raised funds in international bond markets to pay back early some $3.5 billion to the U.S. Treasury and $1.5 billion to the International Monetary Fund.

The funds were loaned to Mexico in February 1995 to shore up the Mexican economy in the wake of a catastrophic devaluation which plunged the country into a deep recession and almost caused it to default.
At the time, the bail-out stirred controversy on both sides of the border. But both leaders said the decision to dig so deep into the public purse was borne out by Mexico's recovery since.
Clinton said the United States made some $580 million in profit on the transaction, and that its exports to Mexico were at an all-time high.

In Mexico, Zedillo said the early repayment would help build on an economic recovery that began last year but has still not been felt by many Mexicans, who continued to suffer from a recession in 1995 that was the worst in living memory.

"The paying off of debts that we've decided on today is one more step toward consolidating the recovery," Zedillo said during a hastily-called ceremony in the presidential palace announcing the loan repayment to top business leaders and financiers.
On cue, Mexico's stock market surged some 1.5 percent on the news that was timed to catch the markets as they opened. The peso was firm, and interest rates continued a welcome downward trend.
Breathless traders, thrilled by the announcement, said it was bound to raise Mexico's standing among foreign investors who have already begun piling back into Mexico this year.
"It has tremendous symbolic significance," said Jonathan Heath, a respected Mexican economist. "It's saying 'We've overcome the crisis and we're almost back to normal.'"
The beauty of the deal, government officials said, was that the $5 billion was raised without dipping into budgeted funds.

In a statement, the Finance Ministry said it was using money to repay the oil-backed loans that was mostly borrowed via a series of jumbo deals in private international markets in currencies such as dollars, yen, marks and lira.
The deal represented the last installment of a series of pre-payments that ranged from $700 million in October 1995 to $1.3 billion in January 1996 to $7 billion in July.
Analysts said it helped the government overcome a pressing repayments schedule that it faces over the next 5-7 years, because it substitutes short-term debt with longer-term bonds.
Those efforts to pay off debts have been bolstered by a windfall profit from high world oil prices.

Heath said the government was also spared from building international reserves because of its floating exchange rate regime, so it could afford to use revenues from bond issues to refinance shorter-term debt.
But despite the payments, Mexico remains the biggest debtor of the IMF, with some $10.5 billion outstanding.
Finance Ministry spokesman Alejandro Valenzuela said the government was currently in talks with the Fund on a medium-term program to refinance its upcoming obligations.
Heath expected those discussions to lead to a three-year extension of its borrowing facility, that he said runs out in February. IMF repayments, however, are scheduled over a longer period.
